question: Carr argues the web encourages one way of reading above others. Which?
answer: Skimming and scanning. Eye-tracking studies he cites found that many web readers move in an F-shaped pattern: across the top lines, then down the left edge, rarely reading a page through. That suits finding facts fast, Carr says, but not the sustained attention that builds understanding.
move: Decide whether you need to find a fact or understand an idea.
trap: 'Slow, careful study': the web holds great writing too.
simply: Online, our eyes do a quick F: read the top, slide down the left side, and move on. Fine for a phone number, not for a big idea.
why: Knowing your default online is skimming helps you switch modes on purpose when something deserves real reading.

book.title: The Shallows
book.author: Nicholas Carr
book.badge: A finalist for the Pulitzer Prize

reference: Nicholas Carr, The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains (W. W. Norton, 2010), ch. 7
